title: Exercise under heat stress: thermoregulation, hydration, performance implications, and mitigation strategies
authors: Periard JD, Eijsvogels TMH, Daanen HAM
population: Comprehensive review of human exercise-heat physiology (thermoregulation, hydration, performance, exertional heat illness) and mitigation strategies
findings: A rise in core temperature and loss of body water by sweating are natural consequences of prolonged exercise in the heat.
Exercise-heat stress disrupts homeostasis, leading to hyperthermia, hypohydration, sodium disturbances and in some cases exertional heat illness.
The review examines the physiological mechanisms (including systemic and peripheral hemodynamic adjustments) by which heat and hypohydration impair performance.
Mitigation strategies reviewed: heat acclimation, cooling strategies and hyperhydration; controversies and future research directions are summarized.
limitations: Narrative, not systematic; no quantitative pooled estimates in the abstract; mostly lab and elite-sport literature, not 100-mile events.
implications: Mechanistic basis for treating heat strain as cumulative (core temperature, hydration), which motivates duration-scaled and effort-based (HR/RPE) heat adjustments instead of a pace penalty alone. This is a design inference, not a quoted finding.
Place heat acclimation first among mitigations, with cooling and hydration as secondary levers; no numeric rule is justified by the abstract.

verification.notes: Crossref (Physiol Rev 2021-10, Periard) and Europe PMC abstract re-fetched. Researcher's quoted findings match. Cardiovascular drift is not named in the abstract, so it is moved out of the findings into a labelled inference.
